title: Chitrakara: service, households and changing work
description: Chitrakara community history through temple responsibilities, household collaboration, apprenticeship and changing markets in Raghurajpur and Danda Sahi.
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy
lead: A finished painting can conceal the people who prepared its surface, drew its figures, completed its borders and carried it to a buyer. Chitrakara history brings those relationships into view. It also asks us to distinguish a community from the wider world of people who practise Pattachitra.

paragraphs.text: Mamata Tripathy’s 1998 Raghurajpur study describes painting as household work. Women’s tasks included preparing glue and chalk and polishing the surface. The account also recalls artists sharing transport when taking paintings to distant buyers.

Tripathy describes three groups, or badas, named for Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra, with responsibilities including supplying their respective anasara paintings. These links between household, community and temple help explain how the work was organised. They are the study’s account, not a complete register of temple duties today.
Preserving this heritage means noticing the work behind the named painter as well as the finished picture.

sections.title: Learning could produce a shared painting

paragraphs.text: In The Two-Headed Deer, published in 1996, Joanna Williams describes children learning within a family or a master’s household. Practice tasks led to painting images drawn by a teacher or completing borders. A large picture could be a group product; a smaller one might be made by one person. She also records different organisations for the work, including Jagannath Mahapatra’s training programme in Raghurajpur and Ananta Maharana’s cooperative in Danda Sahi.
Who drew the image, who completed it, and how does the maker want the collaboration credited?

sections.title: A painting occupation beyond one community

paragraphs.text: The Foundation for MSME Clusters’ May 2008 report lists artist households in Raghurajpur from several communities, including Chitrakara and Khandayat. Its table concerns artist households in that village, not the population of either community across Odisha. The evidence makes a practical distinction: practising Pattachitra does not by itself establish Chitrakara identity.

The report also contrasts market opportunities in Raghurajpur with difficulties in neighbouring Dandasahi, where artisans faced extended credit and distress selling. It discusses training, exhibitions and development support, while warning that success could not be attributed neatly to one intervention. These are dated findings about access and institutions, not permanent characteristics of the people living in either village.
A history of the craft therefore needs to follow buyers, transport and opportunities to learn, as well as materials and style.

sections.title: What the origin accounts can establish

paragraphs.text: Tripathy records Biswakarma descent as mythology and attributes a royal settlement account to a temple chronicle. Neither supplies an independently verified founding date here: the underlying chronicle and land grants have not been inspected.
paragraphs.locator: Printed200; origin accounts distinguished from directly inspected records

paragraphs.text: Williams encounters a different uncertainty at Buguda. Accounts of where its mural painters came from point to Balipadar and Mathura; she leaves their precise origins unresolved. A remembered association with a place is valuable evidence, but it does not become a verified genealogy simply through repetition.
These sources do not establish one founding event. Local service records and attributed family histories remain important for investigating earlier connections.
